newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland sees uncertainty over NATO "waiting rooms".
newsitem.headline: Finland sees uncertainty over NATO "waiting rooms".

text.p: Finland urged NATO on Thursday to show caution in courting new members and said uncertainty over the future shape of the alliance could cause problems in Europe.

Foreign Minister Tarja Halonen said that in talks with visiting Secretary-General Javier Solana she had expressed concern that NATO was setting up a series of "waiting rooms" for membership in developing closer ties with non-member countries.
"I think that NATO should think before it creates any kind of waiting rooms whether (that) will create more new problems than solve old ones," she said.
Solana was on a first official visit to Finland by a NATO head.

Finland, which during the Cold War decades trod a delicate neutral line alongside the Soviet Union, is keen on closer links with the 16-member alliance but says that for now -- in contrast to former Soviet Baltic states -- it does not want to join.
NATO's Partnership for Peace (PfP) agreement, allowing for closer military co-opeation with NATO, is regarded by many east European countries as a "waiting room" for full membership.

Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovenia are expected to be the first to be considered for membership of the now 16-member alliance. The lengthy entry procedure could begin after a summit next year. But a second "waiting room" of other former Warsaw Pact states is also pressing for admittance.

Russia is strongly opposed to expansion of the alliance set up in the 1950s to counter Soviet military power, especially to any suggestion of the inclusion of the Baltic states which occupy territory Moscow has long regarded as strategically essential to its defences.

Finland has stressed Russia should be involved in building a new security map. Russia for its part has declared it would take "appropriate counter-measures" if the alliance moved up to Russian frontiers.
Helsinki is particularly anxious that NATO enlargement should not invite any Russian claim on the Baltics, which still house large Russian minorities.
Solana said NATO aimed to alleviate fears that its enlargement may trigger new security problems.
He said he understood concern that enlargement could create a new security divide, cutting off the Nordic and Baltic area.

"We have already been thinking about mechanisms so that we do not create any division...the moment that a group of countries maybe enter in the first group, and another in the second group," he told a news conference.
Many Finns are still wary of the Russian "bear" they twice fought over their 800-mile (1,300 km) border in World War Two.
